title: What Examiners Want to See in an EE Introduction
summary: Learn what IB examiners expect in an EE introduction, including a focused question, academic context, suitable method, scope, and argument.
body_markdown:
An Extended Essay introduction should establish a **focused research question** , provide relevant academic context, justify the investigation, and explain how the essay will answer the question. Examiners are not looking for a dramatic opening or an extensive history of the topic. They want evidence that the investigation is focused, feasible, methodologically appropriate, and grounded in the registered subject.


During the **IB EE fall term** , particularly September-November, the introduction should evolve from a statement of intention into an accurate account of the research and argument you have actually developed.


### What examiners are assessing


The introduction is required, but it is not marked as an isolated section. Its effectiveness informs the examiner's judgment of your research framework, subject understanding, methodology, and overall coherence.


Examination session Assessment model Connection to the introduction


Up to **November 2026** Five criteria worth **34 marks** The introduction strongly supports **Criterion A: Focus and method** , including the topic, research question, and methodology.


From **May 2027** Five redesigned criteria worth **30 marks** **Framework for the essay** considers whether the question, methods, and structural conventions create an effective framework.


The IB identifies May 2027 as the first assessment session for the revised Extended Essay. Check your examination session before applying a rubric found online. RevisionDojo's[guide to the 2027 EE assessment criteria](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ee-assessment-criteria-explained-2027-guide) explains the changes, while the[official IB Extended Essay update](https://ibo.org/university-admission/latest-curriculum-updates/dp-extended-essay-updates/) confirms the transition date.


Under either model, the introduction must make the investigation intelligible, focused, and academically credible.


### The five things examiners want to see


### A precise research question


The examiner should identify your **research question** immediately and understand its boundaries. Effective questions often specify a period, location, population, text, variable, case, or analytical framework.


For example, “How did social media affect politics?” is too broad. “To what extent did Instagram campaign messaging influence voter engagement among 18-24-year-olds in the 2024 European Parliament election in Germany?” defines the platform, population, event, and location.


Complex wording is not the same as sophistication. Aim for one clear question that permits sustained analysis within the **4,000-word maximum** . The[RevisionDojo research question guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-craft-the-perfect-ib-extended-essay-research-question-8-proven-tips) can help test focus, feasibility, and subject fit.


### Relevant context and significance


Context should provide only what the reader needs to understand the question. This might include an academic debate, historical situation, scientific principle, economic model, or literary concern. If background does not clarify the question, terminology, or importance of the investigation, move it to the body or remove it.


The rationale should explain **why the question deserves investigation** . Academic reasons include evaluating conflicting interpretations, testing a model, examining a meaningful comparison, or assessing a causal claim. Personal interest may explain your choice, but it cannot replace academic significance. Avoid unprovable claims that nobody has studied the issue before.


### A subject-appropriate method


The introduction must explain how you will produce a defensible answer. Methodology varies by registered subject, so generic statements such as “books, articles, and websites will be used” provide little value.


Subject area Useful method preview


Literature Name the primary texts and features to be analysed, such as imagery, narrative voice, or structure.


History Identify the period, key primary and secondary sources, and basis for evaluating interpretations.


Economics Identify the case, relevant theory, data, and criteria for evaluating outcomes.


Experimental science Identify variables, experimental approach, data collection, and method of analysis.


Psychology Identify the relevant theory or debate and how research studies will be selected and evaluated.


Explain what evidence will be examined and why it can answer the question. Consult the IB's[subject-specific Extended Essay guidance](https://ibpublishing.ibo.org/extendedessay/apps/dpapp/guidance.html?doc=d_0_eeyyy_gui_1602_1_e) , since disciplinary conventions matter more than a universal template.


### Controlled scope and argument direction


Clarify which texts, dates, variables, cases, or criteria are included when the research question does not make these limits obvious. You should also indicate the argument's direction without pretending the result was predetermined.


For example: “The investigation evaluates the policy's effects on employment and inflation before weighing regional differences and limitations in the available data.” This communicates reasoning rather than merely listing sections. The[RevisionDojo EE structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-structure-an-extended-essay-ee) can help translate that route into analytical body sections.


### A practical EE introduction structure


The IB does not prescribe a separate word count for the introduction. Concision matters because the section contributes to the overall word limit.


A useful three-part structure is:


1. **Context and significance:** Introduce the narrow academic problem and explain why it merits investigation.
2. **Research question and scope:** State the exact question and clarify important boundaries or definitions.
3. **Method and argument direction:** Explain the evidence, analytical approach, and sequence of reasoning.


This is planning advice, not an official template. Science essays may require greater methodological precision, while literature essays may need careful positioning of the primary texts. The[official IB subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/university-admission/pdfs/ee_subjectbrief_en.pdf) emphasizes coherent, appropriately structured writing rather than a compulsory paragraph pattern.


### Common introduction mistakes


- **Beginning too broadly:** Statements such as “War has affected humanity throughout history” use words without positioning the investigation.
- **Writing an abstract:** The introduction establishes the inquiry; it does not need to summarize every finding. An abstract is not a required structural element in the current model.
- **Promising unused methods:** If you promise interviews, statistical analysis, or three-text comparison, the body must deliver that work.
- **Hiding the question:** State it directly and keep its wording consistent across the title page, introduction, analysis, and conclusion.
- **Mistaking complexity for quality:** Technical vocabulary and long definitions cannot compensate for weak focus. The[IB grade descriptors](https://ibo.org/contentassets/0b0b7a097ca2498ea50a9e41d9e1d1cf/dp-grade-descriptors-en.pdf) prioritize an appropriate question, methods, knowledge, and sustained reasoning.


### What to do from September to November


Revise the introduction as the investigation develops.


- **September:** Confirm your session, registered subject, research question, and source availability. Draft a functional account of your intended scope and method.
- **October:** Compare the introduction with the emerging body. Remove promised evidence you did not use and add boundaries or methodological decisions that arose during research.
- **November:** Read the introduction and conclusion together. The conclusion should answer the exact question established at the beginning through the approach the introduction promised.


Record significant changes in your reflection process, especially when evidence causes you to narrow the question or modify the method. The researcher's reflection space is recommended rather than mandatory; the[RevisionDojo RRS guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ee-rrs-researchers-reflection-space) explains how it can document decision-making.


Before submitting a draft, make the introduction as coherent as possible. Supervisors may provide guidance, but students remain responsible for the writing, and feedback rules restrict draft handling. Review[how EE supervisor feedback works](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ee-how-many-drafts-can-a-supervisor-read) before using this opportunity.


### Final examiner-focused checklist


Check that:


- The research question is visible, precise, and consistent.
- Context leads directly to the question.
- The rationale is academic and credible.
- The method fits the registered subject.
- Evidence and scope are clearly indicated.
- The body carries out what the introduction promises.
- The argument direction shows reasoning rather than a section list.
- Unnecessary quotations, definitions, and general history have been removed.


### Conclusion


What examiners want to see in an EE introduction is disciplined academic planning made visible. Establish the question, context, significance, scope, method, and argument direction without wasting words or overstating the investigation's importance.


During September-November, treat the introduction as a working contract and revise it as the evidence develops. RevisionDojo's EE Support, Coursework Review, and Jojo AI can help test clarity, while subject-specific guides and tutors can support final checks.
